full_judgment:
4. The prosecution examined the informant as P.W. 1 and examined 3 other more witnesses beside the Investigating Officer. The learned Magistrate after recording the deposition of the witnesses found that the charge as levelled against the accused Lal Mia, present petitioner, have been proved beyond all reasonable doubt and found him guilty and convicted and sentenced him as aforesaid. Against that an appeal was preferred before the learned Sessions Judge, Netrokona in Criminal Appeal No. 58 of 1986 but the learned Court refused to admit the appeal on the grounds of limitation. Against that order this revisional application has been moved before this Court and the Rule obtained and he was granted bail. 

 5. Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury, the learned advocate appeared for the petitioner while Mr.M.R.Khan, the learned Advocate appeared for the State. The learned Advocate for the petitioner having taken me through the impugned judgment and the order of conviction and sentence and the papers on records, submitted, that in the instant case, the trial having taken place in absentia without any service of notice upon the petitioner and the accused petitioner, apart from his memorandum of appeal, having filed a separate petition for condonation of delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act supported by an affidavit explaining that he was completely at dark about the case, no process of the court was served upon him for his appearance and the order of conviction and sentence passed against him in absentia, the learned Sessions Judge would have admitted the appeal for that sufficient cause shown and ought to have disposed of the same in accordance with law. He has further submitted that from a clear reading of the impugned order of the court of appeal below it would appear that the court refused the admission of the appeal without assigning any reason, occasioning a failure of justice and, therefore, the said order need to be set aside in Revision and the appeal preferred by the petitioner appellant need be admitted and heard on merits. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the State, on the other hand, has submitted that a right of appeal is a vested right but it needs, to be filed within 30 days which was not done in the instant case. He, however, admitted that the Code of Criminal Procedure or the Limitation Act did not provide any specific period of limitation as to the day from which limitation would be counted, in case of a trial in fact held in the absence of the accused. 

 9. The question whether an appeal is barred by limitation or not or whether he had been prevented by just and reasonable cause in filing the appeal in time is a question of fact to be decided by the relevant court on an application of mind to the facts stated, and by reference to the records after considering the matter in the light of the attending facts and circumstances of each case and the finding arrived at, need be arrived at judicially and not arbitrarily. 

 13. The amended provision of law shall thus, never be ,interpreted as proving a trial behind the back as-of right but always deemed to be held to his knowledge after making it known to him by all possible ways which starts by affixing a notice at his residence for his information and if a trial is held in absentia but to the knowledge of the accused, the convicted person would also be knowing the date on which the judgment was delivered and would be obliged, if wishes to file an appeal, to file it within 30 days from the day of judgment as in all other cases of criminal appeal under the Limitation Act. 

 14. But in case of a trial alleged to have been held without the knowledge of the accused and behind his back and the Limitation Act having not provided any special limitation for appeal in case of such trial in absentia, as if held ex parte by committing fraud upon the court by suppressing notice, it would be in consonance with the principle of natural justice that in such an appeal time would run from the day of appellant's knowledge of the judgment as in section 18 of the Limitation Act in civil matters. Furthermore, extension of time shall always be available if sufficient cause in shown for delay. 

 15. A somewhat similar point came up for decision in the case of Hakim Rai Vs. The State, before a Full Bench of Punjab High Court, reported in A.I.R. 1957 (Punjab) 134. That was a case concerning complaint filed by a court for using a forged document in a proceeding before that court. The complaint was filed in the court of Additional District Magistrate. It was challenged on appeal before the Court of District Judge. The learned District Judge held the appeal to be barred by limitation and dismissed the same. This dismissal of the appeal as time barred was challenged before the High Court the case reported on the ground that the appeal was filed within two weeks of his knowledge of the above order of dismissal. Their Lordships of the Full Bench in the above reported case came to a finding thus:- 

 "It was an appeal before the District Judge arising out of a criminal proceeding for filing of which the Criminal Procedure Code or the Indian Limitation Act do not clearly or specifically prescribe any period. In consonance with the principles of natural justice therefore time in a case like the present would be taken to start from the day of the appellant's knowledge of the filing of the complaint. 

 In every case he would be entitled to extension of time on the score of sufficient cause for his inability to file the appeal in time if any specific period is to be supposed to govern the appeal. I would consequently hold that the appeal of Hakim Rai had been wrongly thrown out as barred by limitation." 

 16. This supports the view I have taken hereinbefore to the effect that for a case where neither the provision of the Criminal Procedure Code nor the Limitation Act clearly prescribed any date from which time would be counted for limitation as to appeal, 30 days time for appeal would be counted from the date of knowledge of the impugned order of conviction. 

 17. In the instant case, it is evident from the record that the learned Magistrate's order of conviction and sentence appealed against was passed on 5.4.86 and the convict was arrested from his village home situated within a different police station on 9.8.86, when according to the petitioner, he all on a sudden came to know of the existing criminal case and consequent order of conviction and sentence. This had not been disputed any where. It is also on record that while he was in custody after 9.8.86 he through his elder brother applied for a certified copy of the judgment and order of the court of the learned Magistrate and he received it on 30.8.86 and the appeal was filed on 1.9.86 and therefore, it is evident that the appeal had been preferred within 30 days from the date of knowledge. This ought to have been considered by the court below while refusing admission of the appeal considering it to be time barred. It appears that the court below in coming to a finding of fact that the appeal is barred by limitation, took a wrong view of the law, which, therefore, cannot be sustained. 

 18. Over and above, under the provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act, the operation of which has not been excluded in the instant case, a person would be entitled to an explanation for the delay. He had explained the same. It appears to be reasonable and sufficient explanation for the delay and moreover, when counted from the day of knowledge there is no delay at all.
